content:
Hello, we are a group at the University of Washington that has been working on a benchmark formalization project, and we would value input from the community. To our understanding, many formalized research benchmarks are in the realm of algebra, with the FATE series, LeanGAP, and a few others that seem to be algebra-focused. Although efforts like Google DeepMind's formal conjectures exist, we notice a lack of formalized mathematics benchmarks in other fields. This is why we propose to formalize LemmaBench, which is a live benchmark that periodically takes newly published research-level lemmas from arXiv papers across mathematics and formalizes their statements.

To be completely transparent about the process, the target would be a carefully checked Lean statement with a single sorry for the proof of the main lemma, i.e., we would prove any sublemmas. We would use a steerable autoformalization pipeline to formalize these statements. Then rigorously check the faithfulness of the statements. We are aware, however, that a faithful formalization requires API that doesn't exist or might be difficult to state correctly (as was found in the Jacobian challenge); in these cases, we would simply leave it out.

We already have a PhD student and a Master's student working on this, and we would be very interested in collaborating with anyone here who finds this idea useful or would like to offer advice.

Concrete questions: (1) Would a research-level Lean benchmark spanning fields beyond algebra benefit the Lean community? (2) Are there major issues with this approach we may be overlooking?

TLDR: We are considering creating a research-level formalized benchmark that is broader than just algebra, and we want to gauge reactions from the Lean community.

Just a heads up that my team in London will be releasing 50 formalised statements of recent theorems from the Annals this week and we're hoping that people find it valuable. One of the main problems we had was that in many modern areas of mathematics mathlib is missing key definitions, and I think that this is the real bottleneck, not "algebra" (whatever that means) -- missing definitions is what restricts formalising statements.
